extracted.intended_audience: early-career researchers applying for the ERC Starting Grant
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for writing an ERC Starting Grant proposal and preparing for the remote review + interview stages, aimed at early-career researchers transitioning to independent group leadership. Covers what panels actually look for, the two-stage evaluation psychology, CV strategy, and interview tactics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 1 screening (Part B1 + CV)
rubrics_metrics.description: Part B1 (synopsis) + CV only are reviewed at Step 1 by generalist panel members; the primary goal is screening and survival to Step 2.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewers are often generalists within the panel domain and use shortcuts. From 2026, feasibility is no longer assessed at Step 1, so B1 must emphasise a ground‑breaking, high-risk/high-gain vision — it must 'scream' revolution rather than incremental progress. Survival rates: only ~25–30% advance to Step 2, so B1 and the CV must signal 'future leader' immediately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 2 deep evaluation & interview
rubrics_metrics.description: If you pass Step 1, the full proposal (Part B2) is reviewed by specialist remote referees and you are interviewed; this is a deep dive into methodology, preliminary data, and claims, and the interview assesses the PI.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specialist referees scrutinise methods, preliminary data, and specific claims. The interview is substantive (25–30 minutes) and decides funding for many candidates (∼40–50% of interviewed candidates get funded). Be prepared to justify methodology, risk mitigation, and your leadership in person.

rubrics_metrics.name: Delegation (track record as proxy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers use 'delegation' — past achievements are proxies to predict future success and reduce anxiety about awarding large grants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trust markers include papers published without your PhD supervisor, competitive fellowships (e.g., Marie Curie), prestigious awards, and other signals of independent achievement. If your CV doesn't immediately signal a future leader, your proposal may not get a deep read.

rubrics_metrics.name: Calibration (relative distinctiveness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers judge proposals relative to the other proposals on their desk, not in isolation; they use 'calibration' to rank and filter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A proposal that's 'solid' for a national grant may look boring against multiple moonshots. You must be distinct — stand out rather than merely be good. Position your idea to distinguish it from competing submissions the panel will see.

rubrics_metrics.name: Articulation (coherence between CV and project)
rubrics_metrics.description: The panel checks whether the 'you' in the CV matches the 'project' in the proposal; coherence between applicant background and the proposed research is essential.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If your background seems misaligned (e.g., a data scientist proposing wet-lab biology), explicitly explain the transition and why your skills make you the right PI. The proposal and CV should tell one coherent story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contribution ('so what?' / ground‑breaking impact)
rubrics_metrics.description: Panels assess the 'contribution' — if the project succeeds, does it change the field or textbooks? The ERC wants research that opens new fields, not incremental extensions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame the expected transformative impact clearly. Avoid descriptions that amount to 'more of the same, but bigger.' Explicitly articulate the novel, field‑changing payoffs of success.

rubrics_metrics.name: PI‑centricity and independence requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: ERC Starting Grant projects must be PI‑centric; independence from PhD/postdoc supervisors is non-negotiable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid language that suggests continuation of a supervisor's programme ('I will continue the work I started in Prof. X's lab...'). Use independent language ('Building on my expertise, I will now open a completely new direction...'). Provide evidence of independence (see 'evidence of independence' metric).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid reliance on collaborators for core work
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposals that rely heavily on collaborators to perform the 'hard parts' are penalised because the ERC is looking for a leader who owns the vision and execution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design the project so the PI demonstrably drives the key scientific advances. If collaborators are essential, make clear what the PI will personally lead and why external expertise is supplementary rather than central to success.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence of independence (concrete markers)
rubrics_metrics.description: Concrete signs that you are independent and can lead the project: last‑author publications, invited talks as guest, research vision that diverges from mentors, awards and fellowships obtained independently.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the CV and narrative CV sections to highlight these markers. If you lack traditional markers, emphasise alternative evidence (e.g., tool adoption, leadership of software or datasets, invited industry contributions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrative CV & DORA-aligned track record presentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Present quality over quantity: ERC follows DORA principles — no impact factors; focus on the content and significance of your best outputs (e.g., best 10 papers). Use narrative CV to explain significance and personal contribution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don't just list publications; explain why each important output matters ('This paper challenged the prevailing dogma on X...'). Use narrative sections to explain career breaks, field changes, industry experience, and non‑traditional outputs (software, tools) as evidence of leadership and suitability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Feasibility assessment occurs later (2026 change)
rubrics_metrics.description: From 2026, feasibility will no longer be assessed at Step 1 and is evaluated at Step 2 by specialists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: At Step 1 emphasise ground‑breaking potential; at Step 2 be ready with robust methodology, preliminary data, and precise risk‑mitigation plans to demonstrate feasibility when specialists scrutinise the technical details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interview strategy: use the time to add value, not recap
rubrics_metrics.description: The interview is not for summarising the proposal; the panel has read your paperwork and wants to assess your vision, leadership, and how you handle critique.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In a 25–30 minute interview: (1) update them on new preliminary results since submission; (2) address known risks and reviewer concerns (e.g., 'Reviewer 2 worried about X. Here is exactly how we solve it.'); (3) show leadership and intellectual maturity. Prepare answers to unwritten questions: 'What is your Plan B if objective 1 fails?', 'Why is this an ERC project and not a national grant?', 'Who are your main competitors?' Maintain confident presentation (speak with authority; don't look at your shoes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Write to two different audiences (generalists then specialists)
rubrics_metrics.description: Your application must first convince generalist Step 1 reviewers, then excite specialists at Step 2; the document must serve both audiences coherently.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Part B1 should be bold, visionary, and readable by non‑specialists; Part B2 must contain the technical depth specialists expect. Ensure the narrative and CV reassure generalists about your leadership while the proposal contains rigorous specialist evidence (methods, preliminary data) for Step 2.

rubrics_metrics.name: CV strategy: every line should support independence
rubrics_metrics.description: Treat the academic CV as a narrative argument: every entry should support your claim to scientific independence and leadership.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Highlight activities demonstrating ownership (last authorship, inviting talks, independent grants), frame industry or non-traditional experience as unique skills, and explain career breaks. Use narrative CV sections to contextualise fewer publications (e.g., major software/tool adoption).

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand eligibility, scheme choice, and timing
rubrics_metrics.description: Selecting the correct scheme and verifying eligibility (e.g., 5‑year rule, career break extensions) is critical; mismatching scheme or missing eligibility rules can disqualify or reduce competitiveness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the ERC eligibility calculator and compare schemes (Starting vs Consolidator vs Marie Curie vs national fellowships). Choose the scheme that matches your career stage and can maximise perceived independence and impact.
